markdown.markdown: - Understand **normal distribution**, e.g. expectation, variance, critical value - Know how to generate the normal random numbers - know how to use `qqplot` to investigate if a variable follows the normal distribution - Know how to use `qnorm` function to find the quantiles of the normal distribution and `pnorm` to find the area under the curve ## Required Packages ```{r, message = FALSE} library(car) library(MASS) ``` ### Tossing Coin Experiment Revisit Suppose we have a fair coin and the probability of getting a head (success) is $p$. Use $X$ to denote the random variable to get a head(1) or a tail(0). Thus **PMF of $X$**: $$ \begin{array}{c|cc} x & 0 & 1 \\ \hline P(X = x) & 1-p & p \\ \end{array} $$ **Expectation and Variance** $$E(X) = (0)(1-p)+(1)p = p,\qquad var(X) = (0)^2(1-p)+(1)^2p -p^2 = p(1-p)$$ Suppose we can generate a sample with sample size 40. Let’s generate samples the replication times 10, 100, and 10000 and investigate the distribution of the sample mean of each sample. ``` {r distrib-of-head,echo=FALSE} n <- 40 x <- c(0,1) sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling10Reps<-replicate(10, mean(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE))) sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling100Reps<-replicate(100, mean(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE))) sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling10000Reps<-replicate(10000, mean(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE))) par(mfrow=c(1,3)) hist(sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling10Reps,main = paste("Sample mean distribution - 10 reps")) hist(sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling100Reps,main = paste("Sample mean distribution - 100 reps")) hist(sampleMeanInRepeatedSampling10000Reps,main = paste("Sample mean distribution - 10000 reps")) ``` Through the experiment, we can see the distribution of sample mean is approximately **normal** with mean equal to the expected value of $X$. In other words, the example above illustrates a known result--**the Central Limit Theorem**, one of the cornerstone results used in inference! ## Normal Distribution The **normal distribution** (also be called *Gaussian distribution*) is a **symmetric** distribution that is centered around a **mean** and spreads out in both directions. Examples: Test scores for all ITMS 514 students. - Notation: $X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ + $\mu$ is the mean of the distribution + $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the distribution - X can take any value on the real line. - Areas under the Normal Curve: \begin{align*} F(x) &=P(X ### Plot Tools to check normal distribution - `qqPlot` in package `car` ```{r,echo = TRUE, message=FALSE} # need "car" package library(car) x <- rnorm(100) qqPlot(x) # Try Petal.Length in iris data set qqPlot(iris$Petal.Length) ``` - `qqnorm` and `qqline` ```{r,echo = TRUE} qqnorm(x, pch = 1, frame = FALSE) qqline(x, col = "red") # For Petal.Length qqnorm(iris$Petal.Length, pch = 2) qqline(iris$Petal.Length, col = "green") ``` #### In-class Exercise: Play with QQ-plot Please use the above plot to investigate `medv` in the data set `Boston` built in `MASS` package. ```{r, message=FALSE} # Please use the following code to access the data set Boston # Need MASS package data(Boston) ``` ### Critical Value **Critical value**: $z_{\alpha}$ of a *standard normal distribution* is the value on the measurement axis for which $\alpha$ of the area under the standard normal curve lies to the right of $z_{\alpha}$. ```{r,echo=FALSE} # Parameters x <- seq(-4, 4, length = 1000) y <- dnorm(x) # Critical value for right-tailed test (alpha = 0.05) alpha <- 0.05 crit_right <- qnorm(1 - alpha) # Plot standard normal curve plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "blue", xlab = "Z", ylab = "Density", main = "Critical Value for α = 0.05 (Right-tailed Test)") # Shade rejection region polygon(c(crit_right, x[x>=crit_right], max(x)), c(0, y[x>=crit_right], 0), col = "red", border = NA, density = 30) # Add reference line abline(v = crit_right, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) # Annotate critical value text(crit_right, 0.02, round(crit_right, 2), pos = 4, col = "red") ``` How to find $Z_{0.05}$ in R? ```{r, echo=TRUE, comment = ''} z0<- -qnorm(0.05, mean = 0, sd =1) z0# display the answer #verify it pnorm(z0) ``` #### Two Tailed Critical Value **Example 2**. Find the value of $z_0$ such that $95\%$ of the standard normal $Z$ values lie between $-z_0$ and $z_0$; that is, $P(-z_0\leq Z\leq z_0) = .95$. **Answer**: \[P(-z_0\le Z \le z_0) = 1- 2P(Z <-z_0) = 0.95 \Rightarrow P(Z<-z_0) = 0.025.\] How to find $z_0$ in `R`? ```{r, echo=TRUE,out.width = "40%",out.height = "40%", comment = ''} z0<- -qnorm(0.025, mean = 0, sd =1) z0# display the answer z0<-qnorm(1-0.025, mean = 0, sd =1) z0 # display the answer #verify it pnorm(z0)-pnorm(-z0) ``` ```{r, echo=FALSE} # Parameters x <- seq(-4, 4, length = 1000) y <- dnorm(x) # Critical values for 95% confidence level alpha <- 0.05 crit_left <- qnorm(alpha/2) # left critical value crit_right <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2) # right critical value # Plot standard normal curve plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "blue", xlab = "Z", ylab = "Density", main = "Critical Values for α = 0.05 (Two-tailed Test)") # Shade rejection regions polygon(c(min(x), x[x<=crit_left], crit_left), c(0, y[x<=crit_left], 0), col = "red", border = NA, density = 30) polygon(c(crit_right, x[x>=crit_right], max(x)), c(0, y[x>=crit_right], 0), col = "red", border = NA, density = 30) # Add reference lines abline(v = crit_left, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) abline(v = crit_right, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) # Annotate critical values text(crit_left, 0.02, round(crit_left, 2), pos = 2, col = "red") text(crit_right, 0.02, round(crit_right, 2), pos = 4, col = "red") ``` #### In-class Exercise: Critical Values 1. Find the value of $z_0$ such that $99\%$ of the standard normal $Z$ values lie between $-z_0$ and $z_0$; that is, $P(-z_0\leq Z\leq z_0) = .99$. 2. Find $z_\alpha$ when $\alpha = 0.01$. ### Conclusion Normal distribution is the most important distribution. When we talk about the Central Limit Theorem, confidence interval, and hypothesis testing, we will come back to the normal distribution.
